READING

**1. Fixing the planning timeline**

The application was validated 2026-08-14. Adding the three benchmarks to that anchor:

| Scenario | Weeks | Consent date | + 22-week build | Occupy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Target | 13 | 2026-11-13 | 2027-04-08 | 2027-04-08 |
| Median | 34 | 2027-03-10 | 2027-08-12 | 2027-08-12 |
| Worst recorded | 61 | 2027-10-15 | 2028-03-17 | 2028-03-17 |

Hallowbrand expires 2027-11-30. For Culverstone to be ready before that date, consent must arrive within approximately 44 weeks of validation (2027-06-22 is the back-calculated latest start date for a 22-week build to finish by 2027-11-30). The published target is 13 weeks; the recorded median is 34 weeks; both sit inside 44 weeks with margin. Only determinations that run materially above median create the Nethercote gap. The worst-on-record case (61 weeks) does produce that gap — roughly 3.5 months from 2027-11-30 to the 2028-03-17 occupation — but that case is by definition the tail, not the centre of the distribution.

The Faskally deposit, once paid, holds the site to 2028-06-30. That date sits 15 weeks past the worst-recorded occupation date of 2028-03-17. The option therefore covers the full range of observed outcomes with a buffer.

**2. What Nethercote actually costs in the worst case**

3.5 months at £18,500/month = approximately £64,750. Add some external maintenance cost for the period without a workshop; call it £15,000–£25,000 for vehicle servicing contracted out over that span. Total worst-case bridging cost: roughly £80,000–£90,000. That is painful but bounded and one-off.

**3. The dead mileage**

Culverstone is 3 miles further each way from Verrancombe Bridge for 22 vehicles on 313 operating days:

22 × 313 × 6 miles × £0.63 = **£26,029 per year**

That is a permanent running cost premium attached to Culverstone for as long as the 44 network is operated from there. Over 10 years it totals approximately £260,000.

**4. Ten-year financial comparison**

Taking the comparable period as the ten years of whichever commitment is made (both courses bind for ten years):

| Item | ARDENSHAW | KESTERWICK |
|---|---|---|
| Rent × 10 years | £2,140,000 | £1,180,000 |
| Capital works | — | £480,000 |
| Non-refundable deposit | — | £40,000 |
| Extra dead mileage × 10 years | — | £260,000 |
| Nethercote bridge (worst case) | — | ~£90,000 |
| **Total (worst-case KESTERWICK)** | **£2,140,000** | **£2,050,000** |

Even with the worst-case Nethercote bridge, KESTERWICK costs approximately £90,000 less over ten years than ARDENSHAW. In the median planning scenario (no Nethercote bridge at all), the saving is approximately £180,000. In the best case it is broadly the same — the works dominate the early years and the rent saving accumulates behind them.

The payback point on the £520,000 capital commitment (deposit plus works), measured against the net annual saving of £96,000 rent minus £26,029 dead mileage = £69,971/year net cash advantage, falls at approximately **7.4 years**. On a ten-year term the surplus beyond payback is roughly £180,000 (median case).

**5. Cash position**

Available funds: £640,000 cash + £200,000 facility = £840,000. The deposit is £40,000 (December 2026), the works are £480,000 (drawn down over the 22-week build, probably in staged payments). Committing both exhausts £520,000, leaving £120,000 cash plus the full £200,000 facility — tight but not dangerous for an operating business generating revenue throughout. The works will be paid largely after rent savings on Culverstone have already begun to accumulate. ARDENSHAW requires no capex but commits the company to £73,000/year more rent than it pays today, an ongoing cash outflow with no terminal value.

**6. The 44/44A bid — the strategically decisive point**

The bid for the next contract term is due 2027-09-14. Depot cost is a fixed line in the submission. In the median planning scenario, Trentmoor is already operating from Culverstone by that date (occupation 2027-08-12). The depot cost it can honestly enter in that bid is approximately £118,000 rent plus £26,029 dead mileage = **£144,000/year**. Under ARDENSHAW the figure is **£214,000/year** — a difference of £70,000 per year in a competitive tender.

That £70,000/year is not a marginal rounding: for a tendered network carrying 22 vehicles the difference either widens the margin on a winning bid or provides the headroom to underbid a competitor whose cost base is higher. The 44 and 44A network employs 22 of the 31 vehicles in the fleet. If the depot cost disadvantage causes Trentmoor to lose that contract at renewal, the financial damage dwarfs the entire Culverstone investment. By contrast, entering the bid with a credible £144,000 depot figure — one already in use because the company moved in six weeks earlier — is a concrete and verifiable number, not a forecast.

In the worst-case planning scenario (consent October 2027), the bid date of 2027-09-14 arrives before consent is granted. This is the one genuinely uncomfortable tension in KESTERWICK. However: the Faskally option is secured and evidenced; the company is still legitimately at Hallowbrand with lease expiry two months away; and the bid can be submitted on the basis of the Culverstone cost structure with a note on anticipated occupation. The bid would be supported by a planning application in progress with a publicly stated 13-week target and a median of 34 weeks. Contracting authorities routinely accept pending-but-probable depot transitions in tender submissions for future contract terms. The alternative under ARDENSHAW — submitting a bid with £214,000 as the fixed depot line — is not uncertain, but it is materially weaker.

**7. What ARDENSHAW actually buys**

Certainty. That is real and not to be dismissed: no planning risk, no construction risk, a workshop from day one, and a known bid number. The cost of that certainty is £73,000/year above current rent, £96,000/year above Culverstone, and a ten-year bond to a landlord who has already shown the appetite to extract a 52% increase on renewal. At the end of ten years Trentmoor will have spent £2.14 million and own nothing at Hallowbrand beyond whatever goodwill it has built with the landlord. It will face a second renewal negotiation from a position of demonstrated dependency.

**8. Qualitative risks specific to KESTERWICK and how they sit**

- *Planning refusal*: Not raised as a risk; the question frames the issue purely as timing. An absolute refusal would change the calculus entirely but is not what the facts put on the table.
- *Cost overrun on works*: £480,000 for hardstanding, fuel island and two-bay workshop is a fixed-price build type. A 10% contingency (£48,000) against the £200,000 facility is absorbable.
- *Workshop gap in worst case*: Serious but manageable for 3.5 months. Scheduled maintenance can be contracted out. Running in heavy vehicles at a third-party workshop for three months is operationally disruptive but not business-threatening for a fleet that also runs school and private hire work.
- *Bid uncertainty in worst case*: As discussed above, this is the sharpest risk but is mitigated by the secured option and the planning application's demonstrable progress.

**9. Synthesis**

The two courses are not genuinely even. ARDENSHAW buys certainty by paying a ten-year premium of approximately £180,000 (median case) or £90,000 (worst case) for it. That premium is real money, but it is the bid dynamics that tip the balance decisively. Entering the September 2027 tender with a depot cost figure of £144,000 rather than £214,000 is the stronger position for the company's core revenue. The planning risk is bounded by a site option that covers even the worst outcome on record. The cash position, while tight after the capital commitment, is not structurally dangerous. The financial arithmetic closes in KESTERWICK's favour in both median and worst cases. The bid arithmetic closes there more emphatically still.

---

READING
The planning application was validated 2026-08-14. The 34-week median determination gives a consent date of around 2027-03-10 and a build completion of 2027-08-12 — inside the Hallowbrand expiry of 2027-11-30 with three and a half months to spare, which means no Nethercote bridge in the central case. The deposit holds the site through 2028-06-30, which covers even the 61-week worst case (occupation ~2028-03-17) with fifteen weeks in hand. The ten-year rent differential is £96,000 per year (£960,000 total); against that, the total KESTERWICK capital and running premium is £780,000 (works £480k, deposit £40k, dead mileage £260k), leaving a net financial advantage of roughly £180,000 in the median case and roughly £90,000 in the worst case. The cash position after committing £520,000 in deposit and works is tight (£120,000 cash plus £200,000 facility) but sustainable for an operating business. The decisive lever is the September 2027 bid: in the median planning scenario Trentmoor is already at Culverstone by the submission date and can enter a depot cost of approximately £144,000 rather than £214,000 — a difference of £70,000 per year in a competitive fixed-price tender for a contract that runs 22 of its 31 vehicles. ARDENSHAW purchases certainty at a price that materially weakens the company's most important competitive tender. KESTERWICK carries planning risk, but that risk is bounded in both probability (median is well inside the safe window) and cost (Nethercote worst case ~£90,000 including maintenance), and the upside in bid competitiveness and long-run cost structure outweighs it.

CALL
KESTERWICK

GROUNDS
The 34-week median planning outcome delivers Culverstone before Hallowbrand expires, the site option covers even the 61-week worst case, and bidding the September 2027 retendering with a depot cost of £144,000 rather than £214,000 is the stronger competitive position for the contract that operates 22 of the 31 vehicles — an advantage that outweighs the bounded planning risk and tight but serviceable post-investment cash position.
